analysis.one_liner: Repeals the oil and chemical excise tax that pays for toxic waste site cleanup.
analysis.headline: The repeal has sat in the Ways and Means Committee since February 2026 with no hearing, no vote, and support only from its six Republican sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end the excise tax, under tax code section 4611, that oil companies pay on petroleum products and chemical makers pay on taxable chemicals. That tax is what feeds the federal Superfund trust fund, which pays to clean up the country's worst toxic waste sites. The bill would also stop the government from making further advances to the fund. The bill takes its name from gas prices, but the petroleum tax it repeals comes to roughly a quarter of a cent per gallon — a fraction of a dollar on a typical fill-up.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil refiners and producers and chemical manufacturers, which would stop paying the Superfund excise tax. Drivers would save only a fraction of a cent per gallon, since the petroleum portion of the tax is charged by the barrel and works out to about a quarter of a cent per gallon.

how_it_helps.text: The bill terminates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate, saying it 'shall not apply after December 31, 2025,' which ends the excise tax on petroleum products and taxable chemicals collected under section 4611 of the tax code.
The bill also ends the Treasury's authority to advance money to the Superfund trust fund, cutting a deadline of 2032 back to the date the bill would be enacted.
Because the petroleum tax is levied per barrel, its repeal would lower pump prices by only about a quarter of a cent per gallon if fully passed through to consumers.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and no further action has been taken on it.

analysis.who_pays: The Superfund trust fund loses its dedicated revenue stream, so cleanup of toxic waste sites slows or shifts to general taxpayer money. Residents near contaminated sites — disproportionately lower-income communities — bear the cost when cleanups are delayed. The savings at the pump for drivers are negligible.
analysis.who_pays_short: Toxic site cleanup, funded by taxpayers instead

drawbacks.text: The bill ends the dedicated funding for the Superfund program, which cleans up the nation's most contaminated hazardous waste sites, by terminating both the tax and the trust fund's advance authority.
Repealing a tax charged to oil and chemical companies shifts the 'polluter pays' funding model for hazardous waste cleanup toward general federal revenue, which comes from all taxpayers.

Supporters' stated benefit — lower gas prices — is small in practice: the petroleum Superfund tax is charged by the barrel and works out to roughly a quarter of a cent per gallon, so repeal would save a driver well under a dollar on a full tank.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost and benefit are badly lopsided. The relief at the pump is a tiny fraction of a cent per gallon, while the bill removes the dedicated money stream for cleaning up toxic waste sites — sites that tend to sit in or near lower-income communities. The tax being repealed is paid by oil and chemical companies, not directly by drivers at the pump in any meaningful amount. The bill is essentially an industry tax cut framed as consumer relief.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee in February 2026, and has not moved since.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Carey introduced the bill on February 12, 2026, with five Republican cosponsors: Reps. Hern, Miller, Malliotakis, and Wied.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No hearing, markup, or vote has been recorded since the referral.
All six original sponsors are Republicans, and no Democrats have joined.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As of now, nothing has changed: the Superfund excise tax is still being collected, so the cleanup fund and the communities it serves are no worse off, and the oil and chemical companies have gained nothing yet. The bill's sponsors have gained nothing either, beyond the introduction itself.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No change yet; the tax still applies

for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate the Superfund financing rate and named it the Pay Less at the Pump Act.

for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and has taken no recorded action on it since February 2026.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred; the only visible signal is that all five cosponsors plus the sponsor are Republicans, with no Democratic support [S3].

industries.note: The bill repeals their per-barrel Superfund excise; that tax passes through to the pump at only about a quarter of a cent per gallon, so consumers would see almost none of the savings while the cleanup fund loses its petroleum revenue.
Section 4611's rate also applies to taxable chemicals, so repeal ends the chemical industry's contribution to the toxic cleanup fund.
With less dedicated Superfund money, government-funded site cleanup work shrinks, reducing demand for cleanup contractors.

analysis.trajectory: With a single-party list of cosponsors, no hearing or markup months after referral, and a contested policy premise, the bill is very unlikely to move on its own. Its most realistic path would be as a rider on a larger tax package; otherwise it dies quietly at the end of the 119th Congress.
